summary: Su's 2010 Berkeley dissertation adds inspector-executor transfers for remote indirect reads and update-by-owner for synchronized writes to the Titanium PGAS compiler, evaluated on clusters against an MPI library and against unoptimized code. It also reports multicore update-strategy tradeoffs in C code and a trace-based tool that finds communication-count bugs at scale.
why_read: It gives a detailed account of how a PGAS compiler turns irregular reads and writes into scheduled or aggregated communication, with measured cluster results.
main_contribution: Compiler analyses and Titanium runtime support that generate inspector-executor transfers for indirect reads and update-by-owner for synchronized-region writes on clusters.
main_limitation: The cluster cost model is point-to-point and ignores network contention, and the write transform relies on associative operators and on Titanium's barrier-based analyses.
evaluation_method: measured speedups vs an MPI library (1-16 processes) and vs unoptimized code (2-128 cores); multicore thread sweeps on three SMPs; trace-based trend fits
states_relationship_to: Chakrabarti et al. (HPF schedules across loops)
Su and Yelick (earlier Titanium communication optimizations)
